name: version-number
intent: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value.
problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.
context: Applies to records that outlive the transaction that read them: edits spanning user think time, a web form round-trip, an offline client, a batch worker holding aggregates, or any read-modify-write over data other writers touch in between. It needs a store that can test the token and change the record in one atomic step (a conditional UPDATE, a compare-and-swap, a document revision check) and a caller willing to act on the conflict - re-read, merge, retry, or report. It assumes conflicts are the exception; when they are the rule a pessimistic lock prevents the wasted work instead.
benefits: Lost updates become observable: the stale write fails with a first-class conflict outcome (StaleDataError, DbUpdateConcurrencyException, StaleObjectError, OptimisticLockException, OptimisticLockError) that the caller must answer, instead of silently discarding another session's work.
No lock is held between read and write: readers and editors are never blocked, which is the only workable option when the gap is a user's think time rather than milliseconds.

Cheap and portable: one attribute per record plus one predicate per statement, with no lock manager, no coordinator and no extra round trip; the same mechanism works over SQL rows, documents and in-memory shared state.
Conflict cost is proportional to conflicts rather than to traffic: writes on unchanged records never pay, and only the writer whose token is out of date is rejected.
The refusal is decidable: the caller gets a definite 'your copy is stale' signal and can re-read, merge field-wise, retry an idempotent command, or ask the user to reconcile.
Composes with a Unit of Work: each dirty record's flush carries its own version predicate, so one stale row aborts the whole commit instead of half-applying it.
tradeoffs: Conflicts arrive as failures after the work has been done: the session must replay, merge or reload, and the pattern itself supplies no resolution strategy.

The guarantee is only as strong as the least careful statement: bulk UPDATE/DELETE, raw SQL, admin scripts, triggers and foreign writers bypass the predicate unless every path is taught the convention.
Extra schema and mapping maintenance: a column or field that every migration, mapper, fixture and write path must carry and must never forget to bump.
Retry storms under contention: frequent conflicts turn into re-read/retry loops that burn CPU while a real lock would have serialised the writers deterministically.
Timestamp-style tokens inherit the storage clock's resolution and skew: a token that is not strictly increasing can miss a change (same tick) or flag a phantom conflict (skewed clocks).
It cannot see write skew: a rule spanning several rows can be violated by two individually fresh writes, because each row's token is still valid.
The token leaks if exposed carelessly: serving it as a public version field or ETag turns an internal concurrency artefact into an external contract that must then stay stable.

participants.responsibility: The per-record version attribute (integer counter, GUID, database rowversion, document revision, sequence number) read together with the data and changed by every write; only its value is compared, never its meaning.
The row, entity or document that carries the token; every in-memory copy remembers the token it was loaded at, and the write path must keep snapshot and token in step.
The statement or operation that changes the record - conditional UPDATE/DELETE, save() through a mapper, or an atomic compare-and-swap - and that carries the token predicate in the same atomic step.
The affected-row count, exchange result or revision comparison that decides whether the token still matched; zero matches or a failed exchange means the copy was stale.

The caller-side policy on detection: re-read and retry, merge field-wise, fail the business transaction, or surface the conflict to the user. The pattern stops at detection and delegates this decision.

Bulk statements, migrations, administrative tools and other writers allowed to change records without the token; each must be declared explicitly, because it silently removes the guarantee for the rows it touches.

use_cases: Web forms and editors: a record is loaded into a page, edited for minutes or hours, then saved - the token makes the stale save fail instead of clobbering the other editor's change.
Distributed workers applying commands to the same entity: the second worker's write is rejected so it can refresh and re-apply, giving first-writer-wins with no held lock.
Data mappers and units of work: every dirty entity flushed at commit carries the version it was loaded with, so the whole transaction aborts on the first stale row.
Document stores and revision-based APIs: Mongoose's __v with optimisticConcurrency, CouchDB-style revisions, or a REST ETag/If-Match precondition all expose the same per-document token.
Leases, leader election and configuration records: one row represents ownership or a monotonic generation, and a write must prove it still holds the revision it acted on.
Offline or mobile sync: clients push edits made against a snapshot taken days earlier, and the version check decides which edits apply directly and which must go through a merge.

Hibernate ORM / JPA @Version: the mapper owns an integer (or timestamp) version property, appends it to every UPDATE's WHERE clause, bumps it on flush and raises StaleObjectStateException / OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, so the application code never writes the predicate by hand.

DynamoDB conditional writes: each item carries a Version attribute; UpdateItem sends ConditionExpression 'Version = :read_value' and increments Version in the same request, and ConditionalCheckFailedException is the conflict signal that triggers a bounded re-read-and-retry — the same contract exposed as @DynamoDBVersionAttribute in the enhanced client.

Cassandra lightweight transactions: UPDATE ... SET col = ? WHERE id = ? IF col = ? is a Paxos-backed compare-and-set, giving the token test linearizable semantics across replicas — at a documented cost (roughly four extra round-trips per conditional write), so it is reserved for rows that genuinely need the guard.
avoid_when: The read-modify-write already runs inside one transaction with a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, repeatable read): the lock excludes the lost update and an additional token adds only maintenance.
Conflicts are frequent or the work between read and write is expensive: a Pessimistic Offline Lock (or Coarse-Grained Lock) prevents the wasted effort instead of merely detecting it.
Set-based writes dominate (mass reclassification, retention deletes, backfills): per-row tokens either explode into per-row statements or are bypassed - give the batch an exclusive window instead.
The store already versions the data for you - an event-sourced aggregate with sequence numbers, an append-only log, a session state that is simply replaced - and a second token adds no information.
There is only one writer at a time (single-threaded batch, exclusive queue consumer, embedded store): stale data cannot exist, so the token is pure ceremony.
anti_patterns: A version column that nothing increments (or that some writers forget): the predicate always matches and the protection is theatre.
Checking the token after the write - re-reading the row 'to see whether it changed' is a separate step and races with exactly the writers the check is meant to catch.
Retry-by-overwrite: catching the conflict and immediately saving the same stale in-memory values again, which converts detection into a delayed lost update.
Using the token as a business key or ordering value: bumping it on unrelated writes, sorting by it, or exposing it as the entity id.
Comparing wall-clock timestamps written by different machines and calling clock skew a conflict policy.
Versioning one row and believing a cross-row invariant (allocation sums, parent/child totals) is protected - write skew needs the aggregate or the isolation level to be guarded.
design_principles: Detect rather than prevent: pay for concurrency only when a conflict actually occurs.
Put the guard and the mutation in one atomic step - a precondition that can be separated from the write is not a precondition.
Make the failure explicit: a stale write must be an observable outcome of the write call, not a log line and not silence.
Give the token one owner (mapper, repository, unit of work); scattered maintenance is how a predicate gets forgotten.
Identifier and token are different things: identity is stable, the version changes on every write and must never be used as identity.
best_practices: Carry the version predicate in the same statement (or compare-and-swap) that performs the write, and branch on the affected-row count or exchange result immediately.
Keep the loaded token with the record snapshot; never re-read the version after the write to decide whether it had been stale.
Define one conflict policy per use case - retry after re-reading, merge field-wise, or fail the transaction - and never retry with stale values.
Confine the token to persistence, or expose it deliberately as a concurrency precondition (ETag/If-Match); never as a domain attribute or ordering key.
In a unit of work, test every flushed record and abort the whole transaction on the first conflict rather than committing the rest.
Audit non-standard write paths (bulk statements, admin tools, migrations, triggers) and either make them token-aware or declare them exempt.
Prefer a strictly increasing integer or a database-generated rowversion over wall-clock timestamps; if a timestamp or GUID is used, document its resolution and ordering assumptions.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Optimistic Offline Lock (Offline Concurrency Patterns, ch. 16), which prescribes the version number (or timestamp) token as its conflict check.
